title: Profiling and Debugging
description: Profile and debug React Query performance using DevTools, query inspectors, and network analysis.

data.text: Before optimizing, you need to measure. React Query provides first-class DevTools that show query status, cache state, and performance timing. Combined with browser network inspection and React Profiler, you can identify slow queries, memory leaks, and unnecessary re-renders with precision.

The DevTools panel gives you a live view of every query and mutation in your application. You can inspect query keys, status, data, and timestamps. In development, DevTools automatically appear in the bottom-right corner. In production, you can disable them or enable them conditionally.

data.title: Conditional DevTools
data.text: Wrap the DevTools component in a process.env.NODE_ENV check or feature flag so it never ships to production accidentally.

data.title: Setting up React Query DevTools
data.content: Mounting the DevTools panel in your application root

data.text: Each query in DevTools shows its current state: `pending`, `success`, or `error`. You can see the exact data object, the query hash, and the time since last fetch. If a query is stuck in `pending` or `error`, DevTools helps you identify whether the issue is network-related, a bad query key, or an exception in the query function.

data.text: React DevTools Profiler records render timings and commit data. Use it alongside React Query DevTools to see which components re-render when queries update. If a parent re-renders and passes new props to a memoized child, the profiler flags the mismatch. Common culprits are inline object literals, array spreads, and unstable callbacks.

data.caption: Systematic debugging flow for slow React Query applications
data.definition:
graph TD
    A[Symptom: Slow UI or Stale Data] --> B{React DevTools Profiler}
    B -->|Excessive renders| C[Check props and memoization]
    B -->|Normal renders| D{React Query DevTools}
    D -->|Stale queries| E[Check staleTime and gcTime]
    D -->|High refetch rate| F[Check query keys and refetchOnWindowFocus]
    D -->|Cache misses| G[Check query key consistency]
    C --> H[Apply useMemo / useCallback]
    E --> I[Increase staleTime]
    F --> J[Disable refetchOnWindowFocus for hidden tabs]
    G --> K[Standardize query key factories]
    H --> L[Measure again]
    I --> L
    J --> L
    K --> L

data.text: Browser DevTools Network tab reveals what React Query is actually requesting. Look for duplicate requests, missing cache headers, and slow response times. Combine this with `queryClient.getQueryData()` to inspect the cache programmatically and verify that data is stored under the expected keys.

data.title: Inspecting the cache programmatically
data.content: Using the QueryClient to inspect and manipulate cache during debugging

items.text: Open React Query DevTools and scan for queries stuck in pending or error state
items.hint: A high error count usually indicates bad query keys or network issues.

items.text: Record a React Profiler session and look for components rendering more than expected
items.hint: Focus on the render count column, not just total time.

items.text: Check Network tab for duplicate requests to the same endpoint
items.hint: If the same queryKey fires twice, check for missing dependencies in useEffect or useQuery.

items.text: Verify staleTime is set appropriately for your data freshness requirements
items.hint: A staleTime of 0 means every window focus refetches.

items.text: Log query cache size in development to catch memory leaks
items.hint: A growing cache with no gcTime limit can exhaust browser memory.

items.question: Why does my query refetch when I switch tabs?
items.answer: By default, React Query refetches when the window regains focus. Set refetchOnWindowFocus: false in query options if your data does not need real-time freshness.

items.question: How do I find which component triggers a refetch?
items.answer: Use the Query Log in React Query DevTools. Each log entry includes the component stack trace showing which useQuery instance triggered the fetch.

items.question: Is the DevTools panel available in production?
items.answer: Yes, but you should only ship it when explicitly needed. Wrap it in process.env.NODE_ENV === 'development' or a feature flag.

data.title: Debug a Slow Query Using DevTools
data.description: A product listing page loads slowly. Use React Query DevTools and React Profiler to identify the bottleneck.
steps: Open React Query DevTools and identify the slow query
Check if the query is stuck in pending or refetching unnecessarily
Open React Profiler and record a render while the page loads
Identify which components re-render more than expected
Check Network tab for duplicate or slow requests
Apply the fix and verify in DevTools that the query status improves
data.expectedOutcome: Identify the root cause (e.g., missing staleTime, duplicate query key) and resolve it.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: React Query DevTools provides real-time visibility into queries, mutations, and cache state
React Profiler identifies unnecessary re-renders caused by unstable props
Browser Network tab confirms actual HTTP behavior
Programmatic cache inspection with getQueriesData helps validate key consistency
data.takeaway: Profiling is not a one-time task. Build a habit of checking DevTools during development to catch performance regressions early.
